meta.title: The First 90 Days
meta.subtitle: Scenario 53 — Every Bed in the County (a fictional composite)
meta.summary: You are Cyrus. Your three children have been in care since February 2nd of last year — Selah, twelve, in one foster home; Rafi, nine, and Nina, five, in another, forty minutes apart. Your mother Esther said in March she could take Nina. Only Nina. On May 2nd your children reach fifteen months in care, and the law's permanency clock strikes. This scenario is about what gets built before it does.

nodes.title: Month twelve
body: The letter from the agency is polite and has a date in it, which makes it not polite at all: a permanency review is scheduled for April 22nd, and the children's time in care — placed February 2, 2026 — will reach fifteen months on May 2, 2027. Fifteen months is not an anniversary. Under the federal Adoption and Safe Families Act, when a child has been in foster care for 15 of the most recent 22 months, the state must file to terminate parental rights or document a statutory exception (42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(E)).
You have three children in two houses and one grandmother who said a sentence in March that the file turned into a wall. The next sixteen weeks are this scenario.

choices.text: Read the letter twice. Then call your counsel — appointed under 42 Pa.C.S. § 6337 — and ask the only useful first question: "What are the three exceptions, exactly, and which ones could this family actually build?"

nodes.title: The three doors
body: Your counsel, Mr. Zielinski, keeps a yellow pad for arithmetic. "Door one: the child is being cared for by a relative. Door two: a documented compelling reason that filing isn't in the child's best interest. Door three: the agency didn't provide the services it was supposed to provide. Door one is the strongest, because it isn't an argument — it's an address. Whose address?"

"My mother's," you say. "For one of them. In March she said she could take Nina. The file says she 'declined placement.'" Mr. Zielinski puts his pen down in the particular way lawyers do when a case changes shape. "Then the first fight is about what your mother actually said."

choices.text: Get the record. All of it — your written request under 55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d) goes in this week, aimed first at the March kinship notes.

nodes.title: Two kitchens
body: January's visits are a geography lesson you did not enroll in: Saturdays at the Millersville home with Selah — braiding, homework, her art portfolio — and Sundays in Quarryville with Rafi and Nina, forty minutes and one transfer of a sleeping five-year-old between the two halves of your family. The children spend their sibling time in your car, which has become, by default, the family's only shared room.

Rafi, buckled in the back with Nina asleep on his shoulder, delivers the review's whole question early: 'Dad. Why can't Grandma's house be the house? She has the big table.' The big table seats eight. Everyone in this case knows it. The file, so far, does not.

choices.text: Get the record — the March kinship notes first. If the file can't answer Rafi, the file is the problem to fix.

nodes.title: What March actually said
body: The March note, when it arrives, is three lines: 'Paternal grandmother contacted. States she could take the youngest 'if it comes to that.' States three is too many with her arthritis. Declined placement of sibling group.' Read it again: she answered a question about all three, at once, in a cold call, three weeks after the children were taken — and the answer to that question got filed as the answer to every question.
Nobody lied. A narrower question was simply never asked: not 'all three, tonight, alone forever' — but 'what could you take, with what help, starting when?'

choices.text: Write the correction: a letter for the file stating what Esther was asked, what she answered, and that she is now asking to be studied for a plan — with supports — for all three.

nodes.title: The cost, itemized
body: Before the correction goes in, you do the accounting nobody at the agency is doing: the sibling set's documented contacts since placement — visits between Selah and the younger two, eleven in eleven months, most of them in your car; two missed for weather; one canceled by a schedule change nobody relayed. Eleven meetings a year is not a sibling relationship. It is a pen pal arrangement with snacks.
Mr. Zielinski adds the accounting to the correction letter as an exhibit. 'Courts respond to arithmetic they can check,' he says. 'Ours checks.'

choices.text: File the correction with the arithmetic attached — what Esther was asked in March, and what the split has cost since.

nodes.title: Asking the narrower question
body: Esther, at her kitchen table, is precise about her own limits, which is why she can be trusted about her capacity: "Three children, alone, at sixty-nine, with these hands — no. Three children with the after-school program at the church, with your sister doing Saturdays, with you twelve minutes away and off the truck route by five — ask me that question."
A kinship plan with supports is not a smaller promise. It is a specified one. The study that follows will test the specification, which is why every support has to be a document, not a hope.

choices.text: Build the support plan as paper: the church program's letter, your sister's signed Saturday commitment, your employer's route letter.

nodes.title: Esther, precisely
body: Your mother, asked the narrower question at last, answers it like an engineer: her hands are good in the morning and poor by eight; the stairs are the problem, not the children; she can cook for five standing on one hip and has; what she cannot do is be the only adult in the story — and with the church program, your sister's Saturdays, and you off the truck by five, she would not be. 'I said no to drowning,' she tells you. 'Nobody asked me about swimming with a rope team.'
The support plan is how a rope team gets documented.

choices.text: Build it as paper — every support a letter, every letter signed.

nodes.title: The plan, specified
body: Three letters, three signatures, three phone numbers. The after-school program confirms Selah and Rafi weekdays until six, Nina in the preschool room. Your sister commits Saturdays in writing 'for as long as it takes, which is what family means.' Your employer's letter moves your last delivery to 4:40 p.m. The pile is thin and total: it converts 'Esther plus hope' into 'Esther plus a system.'

Ms. Nilsen, the children's worker, receives the packet with the expression of a woman whose March note just became a January plan. "A resubmission," she says. "New study, based on the plan. I'll schedule it."

choices.text: "Schedule it with dates. Study visit, clearance renewals, report — I want the dates in a letter."

nodes.title: The director's letter
body: The church after-school program's director — who has known Selah since Vacation Bible School and Rafi since he was a rumor — signs her letter at the folding table where the program does its homework: capacity for all three, weekdays to six, Nina in the preschool room with the same teacher her cousin had. 'Families like yours are what the program exists for,' she says, 'though usually the forms are shorter.'
The forms are never shorter. That is why the letters matter: a support that exists as a signature cannot be waved away as a hope.

choices.text: The plan is specified: program, sister, employer. The agency schedules the study — with dates this time.

nodes.title: Dates, in a letter
body: The letter that comes lists them: home visit February 9th; Esther's updated clearances filed; interviews with each child; report due March 20th. Between now and the report sit three problems you already know about: the stairs to the bedrooms and Esther's arthritis; Nina's preschool transport; and the person this scenario has been avoiding — Selah, twelve years old, who has her own opinion and, it turns out, her own lawyer.
Children have counsel too. Selah's has requested a meeting. With you.

choices.text: Go. Listen more than you talk. She is not a obstacle to the plan; she is one of its authors.

nodes.title: Nina's mornings
body: The study's smallest open question is a five-year-old's morning: Nina's preschool is near the Quarryville home, not Esther's. Her teacher, consulted, provides the answer in writing — a mid-year transfer to the sister preschool two streets from Esther's, same curriculum, a seat held on the director's word — and Esther's neighbor, retired, signs on for the walk-to-school run on program days.
Permanency files are lost on questions this size more often than on law. Each unanswered 'but who handles—' is a stone in the approval's shoe. You are removing stones in writing, one at a time.

choices.text: Stones out. Next: the person this case has been avoiding — Selah, and her own counsel's requested meeting.

nodes.title: Selah's position
body: Selah's counsel lays it out with the care of someone translating, not negotiating. "Selah loves her grandmother. She also has a life: her school, two years in the same building, the art teacher who wrote her a recommendation, and a foster mother who taught her to braid and shows up. She is asking: why does helping Rafi and Nina require her to be the one who moves?"

It is the best question in the case, and it is asked by a twelve-year-old through a lawyer, which is how this system hears children when it hears them at all. The answer cannot be 'because the clock.' It has to be an address that keeps her life intact — or an honest acceptance that her door is a different door.

choices.text: Ask the factual question before the emotional one: "What school district is my mother's house in — and is it Selah's?"

nodes.title: One district
body: It is. Esther's house sits in the same school district as Selah's foster home — geography's small mercy, verified in writing from the district office at your request, because in this scenario nothing is true until it is paper. Selah could move to her grandmother's and keep her school, her art teacher, and her recommendation.
What she cannot keep, if she moves, is the daily presence of the foster mother — unless the plan keeps that too.

choices.text: Ask Selah's counsel to put Selah's terms to her precisely: same school guaranteed, monthly overnight with her foster mother, her art portfolio wall at Grandma's — and her answer given the weight it deserves.

nodes.title: Rafi's therapist
body: Rafi's therapist — the one constant adult across his two placements — writes the letter Mr. Zielinski calls the packet's quiet bomb: the sibling separation is 'the presenting theme' of Rafi's sessions; his drawings are an atlas of two houses and a car; unification with his sisters at a stable kinship home is 'the single intervention most likely to change this child's trajectory.'
It is addressed to the court, signed, and — because you requested records and read them — impossible for the agency's packet to omit without noticing its absence.

choices.text: With the district's letter in hand and Rafi's beside it, Selah's terms get put to her in full.

nodes.title: Her terms
body: Selah's answer, when it comes back through her counsel, is a twelve-year-old's treaty: yes to Grandma's — if the school letter is real, if the overnights are written into the plan and not 'when possible,' and if nobody makes her call it anything but what it is: a move she chose with conditions, not a rescue she was handed. She also asks to keep braiding lessons. Some conditions are just love with appointments.

Mr. Zielinski writes the terms into the placement proposal verbatim. "Courts can smell when an adult paraphrases a child into compliance. We will not be doing that. Her words, her conditions, addressed one by one."

choices.text: File the proposal: Esther, all three, supports specified, Selah's terms attached and answered.

nodes.title: The test weekend
body: Selah spends a February weekend at Esther's before anyone files anything final — her own condition, conveyed through counsel: 'I want to sleep there before I say yes to living there.' The weekend runs on her treaty's terms: her corner of the room, her portfolio on the wall, pancakes at the big table with her siblings orbiting, and Sunday braiding with her foster mother by video call, so the two halves of her life can see each other being decent.

Her report back, through counsel, is one sentence: 'Grandma's house is loud in the right way.' The proposal gets filed with that sentence in it, attributed, verbatim. Courts have decided harder questions on less honest evidence.

choices.text: File the proposal — Esther, all three, supports specified, Selah's terms and her sentence attached.

nodes.title: The study visit
body: February 9th arrives with a worker, a tape measure, and Esther's house scrubbed to surgical brightness. The rooms pass. The clearances pass. The stairs do not — not as a failure of the house, but as a question: a sixty-nine-year-old with arthritis, three children, bedtime upstairs. The worker writes 'mobility — plan?' in the margin and keeps walking, which is the study system working exactly as it should: a question, asked in time to be answered.

Your answer takes ten days and a contractor cousin: a first-floor room — the dining room, which has hosted four dinners a decade — converted to Esther's bedroom, with the bathroom beside it. The children get the upstairs. The stairs become the children's problem, and children are stair professionals.

choices.text: Convert the room. Document it: photos, the cousin's invoice, and Esther's doctor's note confirming the arrangement.

nodes.title: The art teacher's letter
body: Selah's art teacher — the one who wrote her recommendation — adds the school's voice to the file: Selah's portfolio is entered in the regional show; her attendance is perfect; 'her stability this year, in one school, is the platform her work is built on,' and the district's letter confirming Esther's address is in-district 'means the platform holds.' Teachers write the evidence permanency law wishes it always had: what a child's life is actually made of, in the present tense.
The study packet grows; the study itself hits its one snag the same week.

choices.text: The snag: Esther's clearance renewal flags an old address mismatch. Correct it with documents, the family's new reflex.

nodes.title: The mismatch
body: Esther's clearance renewal flags an address from 1998 — a house she sold before Rafi's foster parents met — because databases, like families, keep everything and date nothing. The correction is a deed, a tax record, and a letter, assembled by you in four days and transmitted with the same unglamorous ceremony as every other fix in this case: hand-delivered, copy kept, receipt obtained.

It is worth pausing on the pattern, because the pattern is the pedagogy: paper problems are not character verdicts. They are errands with deadlines, and they yield to exactly one method — documents, delivered, confirmed.

choices.text: Errand run. The study visit's written findings are next — and they contain the stairs question, formalized.

nodes.title: Interim findings
body: The study's interim findings arrive as a document instead of a conversation, which your winter has taught you to prefer: rooms adequate; supports verified; clearances clear as corrected; one item open — 'primary caregiver sleeping quarters on second floor; mobility plan required.' Formal questions are gifts: they can be answered formally, in a form the final report must then acknowledge.
Esther reads the item and snorts. 'Required. At last, a form that talks like my doctor.' Her doctor is next.

choices.text: Get the doctor's note — arthritis managed, ground-floor living recommended — and put the conversion plan in writing.

nodes.title: The doctor's note
body: Esther's physician of twenty years writes it in the plain style of a man who has filled out forms since before they were PDFs: arthritis bilateral, managed; stairs inadvisable as a daily routine; 'patient fully capable of caregiving in a ground-floor living arrangement, which I recommend.' It is the medical third of the stairs answer. The carpentry third is your cousin's crew. The documentary third is the addendum the study will now have to write.
You schedule the conversion for the following week. The dining room has hosted four dinners a decade; it is about to become the most important room in three childhoods.

choices.text: Convert the room. Document it: photos, invoice, the doctor's note stapled to the plan.

nodes.title: Problem, answered
body: The study's addendum records the conversion in the flat prose that moves courts: 'Mobility concern addressed; primary caregiver sleeping quarters relocated to first floor with adjacent bath.' Underneath the prose is the recurring arithmetic of kinship: a problem found early is a project; the same problem found at the hearing is a reason.
Two voices remain to be reckoned with, and both belong to people who have loved your children daily: Rafi and Nina's foster parents.

choices.text: Ask Ms. Nilsen what their position will be at the review — and do not flinch from the answer.

nodes.title: Your own file
body: Your track advances in parallel and in writing: the parenting program's certificate, filed; the route change confirmed by your employer's second letter; your visits — all of them, both kitchens — logged by two foster homes as consistent and calm. None of it is the April question, and all of it is the April weather: a court deciding whether to build a permanency plan around a grandmother also reads the father's trajectory for what happens after.
Mr. Zielinski files your progress with the packet without commentary. Trajectories speak in their own tense.

choices.text: Now the reckoning you have been postponing: Rafi and Nina's foster parents, and what they will say.

nodes.title: The other attachment
body: Rafi and Nina's foster parents have had the two youngest for a year. Nina calls their dog by a name she invented and believes is its real name. They will be heard at the review — foster parents receive notice of hearings and have the right to be heard (42 Pa.C.S. § 6336.1) — and what they will say is honest: the children are attached; another move is another loss; they are willing to keep both children 'as long as needed.'

This is the part of kinship work that slogans skip. Their love is real evidence, and it will be weighed. What answers it is not denying it — it is the documented whole: siblings together, with family, in one district, on terms the eldest set herself.

choices.text: Propose the bridge in writing: Rafi and Nina keep monthly visits with their foster parents, written into the plan — continuity, not erasure.

nodes.title: Saturdays at the big table
body: The agency — prodded by your written request and, in fairness, by its own worker's conscience — starts sibling Saturdays at Esther's in March: all three children, her house, the big table, agency transport both ways. The visit notes accumulate the evidence no expert can manufacture: Nina napping in the first-floor room's doorway 'because that's where everyone is'; Rafi teaching Selah the Quarryville dog's invented name; the fort, constructed in Esther's living room under Rafi's generalship, with Selah as minister of blankets.
Saturdays are the placement's rehearsal, documented weekly. By April, the file no longer describes a proposal. It describes a household that already meets on weekends and is asking to stop commuting.

choices.text: Propose the bridge to the foster parents in writing — continuity after the move, not erasure.

nodes.title: Continuity, not erasure
body: The foster parents receive the written proposal through the agency and respond in kind, in writing, with a sentence Mr. Zielinski reads twice: 'If the court moves them, we will help them land. We ask that the landing include us, a little, for a while.' It is the sound of a system working at its best — attachments treated as assets to be transferred, not territories to be defended.

March 20th, the study report issues: Esther approved for the sibling group of three, with the support plan incorporated by reference. The paper part of door one — the relative exception — is now buildable.

choices.text: Ask Mr. Zielinski to draft the ASFA exception documentation for the April review: children to be cared for by a relative, placed before the fifteen-month date.

nodes.title: The agency, of two minds
body: Ms. Nilsen supports the placement and says so in her report draft; her supervisor's margin asks the question supervisors are paid to ask: 'Selah — is the yes durable?' It is a fair question, and it has a documentary answer — her terms, met item by item; her test weekend; her sentence about the loud house — which Mr. Zielinski assembles into a two-page response filed before the review, so the durability question is answered with dates instead of reassurances.
Agencies are not monoliths; they are arguments between a worker's knowledge and a supervisor's caution. Filing for the supervisor's question is how families join that argument on the winning side.

choices.text: Draft the ASFA exception documentation with Mr. Zielinski — door one, built of paper.

nodes.title: Door one, documented
body: The exception paperwork is almost anticlimactic, which is its virtue: if Selah, Rafi, and Nina are placed with their grandmother before May 2nd, the statute's relative-care exception is satisfied by the placement itself, and the filing obligation the clock creates is answered with an address and a date (42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(E)). The review on April 22nd is where the placement must be ordered — ten days before the clock strikes.

What remains is the agency's recommendation, and agencies recommend what their files make easy. Mr. Zielinski inventories yours in the office, the week before: study approved; supports signed; Selah's terms answered; bridges offered; March corrected. "There is one more document," he says, "that I want in the judge's hands. The children's own words — collected by their counsel, not by you."

choices.text: Their counsel collects them. You do not rehearse, coach, or even ask what was said. Some pages must arrive clean.

nodes.title: March 20th
body: The study report issues on the date the January letter promised — a small miracle of the calendar that you note because you have learned to: promises kept by systems are data too. Esther: approved for the sibling group of three, the support plan incorporated, the mobility item closed by the conversion addendum. The agency's recommendation for April is drafted to match, with the supervisor's durability question attached as answered.
What remains is the children's own words, collected cleanly — and April's ordinary weather.

choices.text: Their counsel collects the words. You do not ask what was said. Clean pages only.

nodes.title: Clean pages
body: What the children said becomes known to you only as the court will know it: Rafi asked if Grandma's house has 'room for the fort.' Nina asked about the dog. Selah restated her terms and added one: 'Tell them I said yes myself.' The statements are filed by their counsel as the children's position, and your disciplined absence from them is what makes them evidence instead of choreography.
April approaches with the docket's ordinary weather: a continuance scare, resolved; a supervisor's signature, obtained; a school letter re-verified. Then the 22nd.

choices.text: Go in with the file you built. It is, in the end, the argument.

nodes.title: The scare, again
body: The continuance scare arrives on schedule, as continuance scares do: a scheduling conflict, a floated May date — May, past the clock, which would convert this entire winter into a termination filing answered too late. Mr. Zielinski opposes on the papers the same day, with the ASFA date in the first paragraph and the completed study in the second. The court keeps April 22nd in a short order that does not disguise its reasoning: 'The children's fifteen-month date is May 2nd. The review will be heard April 22nd.'
Even the scare did work: it made a judge write the clock into an order, which means the clock is now the court's own concern and not only yours.

choices.text: One more document surfaces before the review — the agency's own ASFA planning memo. Read it carefully.

nodes.title: The agency's memo
body: The agency's internal ASFA memo — produced with the updated record your January request set in motion — is the winter's most instructive document: it lists the May 2nd date, the three exceptions, and a caseworker's annotation beside 'relative care': 'Grandmother approved 3/20; placement pending court order — exception expected to be satisfied.' Expected. The agency is planning around the same door you built. Its lawyers will nonetheless argue caution at the review, because institutions argue caution the way rivers argue downhill.
You do not confront anyone with the memo. You file your packet so that the court's questions meet it naturally.

choices.text: Assemble the final packet with Mr. Zielinski — every document this winter produced, in chronological order.

nodes.title: The packet
body: Chronology is the packet's argument: March's sentence and January's correction; the specified plan and its signed supports; the district's letter and Selah's treaty; a therapist, a teacher, a doctor, a director; a converted room; eleven Saturdays of visit notes; an approval dated March 20th; and a memo in the agency's own hand expecting the exception to be satisfied. Mr. Zielinski binds it without a summary. 'Summaries are for cases that need adjectives,' he says. 'This one has dates.'
Esther has been ironing for two days. The review is Thursday.

choices.text: The night before: your mother's kitchen, the big table, three empty chairs that may not be empty long.

nodes.title: The night before
body: Esther sets the big table for nobody — for luck, she says, the way sailors set a watch. Your sister calls from her Saturday shift to say the commitment letter is the truest thing she has ever signed. Selah, by her counsel's forwarded message, has added nothing to her terms and withdrawn nothing: 'Tell them I said yes myself. Still.'

You sleep the way litigants sleep, which is to say in shifts, and dream of a car with no children asleep in the back because the children are, at last, already home. Thursday will grade the dream against the file. The file is ready to be graded.

choices.text: Go in with the file you built. It is, in the end, the argument.

nodes.title: April 22nd
body: The courtroom is crowded with your children's lives: Esther in her good dress, approved and documented; the foster parents, heard under § 6336.1, saying their honest piece and their written bridge; Selah's counsel stating Selah's terms and Selah's yes; the agency, Ms. Nilsen presenting, with a recommendation that the last four months either built or didn't.
The judge looks up from the packet. "The fifteen-month date is May 2nd. Counsel, tell me why this court is not looking at a filing obligation — or tell me about the filings."

choices.text: Let Mr. Zielinski answer with the file. It is the moment the file was built for.

nodes.title: May 2nd, answered in April
body: The answer depends on which doors the winter actually built — a relative's address, a child's own terms, or only an argument.

choices.text: Esther is approved for all three, the supports are documents, Selah's terms are in the plan, and placement can occur this week — before the clock: the relative exception, satisfied by placement.
The younger two are ready for Esther's; Selah's terms could not be met, and she stays — by her own stated choice, documented, with her siblings twenty minutes closer than before.
No placement is ready, but the exception and compelling-reason documentation is complete and filed, answering the clock while the plan continues.
The file reaches April thin — a March sentence uncorrected, a study still pending, a child unheard.

nodes.title: Ending — All Three, One Table
debrief: Placement is ordered for Friday, April 23rd — nine days before the clock. Selah keeps her school and gets her overnight clause in writing; Rafi gets a yard with fort jurisdiction; Nina gets a grandmother and, by written bridge, keeps a little of the dog. When May 2nd arrives, it finds the children where the statute's first exception contemplates: being cared for by a relative (42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(E)). No petition is filed, because the law's filing duty is answered by the placement itself.

Inventory the win, because it was assembled, not granted: a March sentence corrected with the March record (requested under 55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d)); a grandmother's capacity specified as a system of signed supports rather than asserted as a virtue; a mobility problem converted into a converted room; a twelve-year-old treated as an author rather than an obstacle — her terms taken verbatim, her school verified in writing, her yes obtained instead of assumed; and foster attachments bridged rather than bulldozed, with the foster parents heard as § 6336.1 provides. Each piece is a document. The stack of documents is the outcome.

What no strategy controls: Esther's health across the years this plan must run, Selah's heart across the first hard month, and a judge who might have weighed the foster attachments differently on the same packet. ASFA's clock is often described as the parent's enemy. This scenario's truer lesson: the clock is a deadline, and deadlines reward the side that builds toward them. The agency had a calendar. This time, so did the family.

nodes.title: Ending — Two Home, One by Choice (partial)
debrief: Rafi and Nina move to Esther's on Friday. Selah does not — and the order says why, in her counsel's words, not an adult's summary: her terms could not all be met this spring, and she elects to remain where she is, with sibling time doubled, Esther's house as her second address, and the question expressly preserved for the next review. The relative exception covers the two who moved; Selah's permanency takes the documented-compelling-reason road, with her own statement as the documentation.

Call this what it is: a partial win with an honest spine. The system's easiest story — 'the grandmother took the little ones; the teenager was left' — is false here, and the record proves it false: Selah was offered the move on terms she set, the terms were pursued, and her no was treated as information rather than defiance. In dependency law, an older child's documented choice is not a failed placement. It is permanency planning done at the speed of consent.
The next review inherits a running household, two settled children, and a teenager whose trust was kept. Families reunify in stages more often than in single orders. This stage was built correctly.

nodes.title: Ending — The Clock, Answered (partial)
debrief: No beds move in April — but no petition is filed in May either. The court accepts the documentation: Esther's approval finalized in principle, the placement plan dated, and the compelling reasons written with specificity rather than incantation — which is what the exceptions in 42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(E) actually require when they apply: not that the clock be ignored, but that its exceptions be documented like facts instead of hoped like weather.

This is the ending for families whose facts are strong and whose timing is not, and it is a real outcome, not a consolation: the difference between a documented exception and an undocumented intention is the difference between a plan and a termination petition. Many cases are lost precisely here — an exception that existed in the family's living room but never made it into the agency's documentation.

The work continues with the clock answered: the study completes, the placement follows in June, and the next review reads a file that treats May 2nd as a date that was prepared for. Prepared-for is the entire discipline.

nodes.title: Ending — Fifteen Months
debrief: May 2nd arrives with the children still in two foster homes, Esther's study still pending, and a March sentence still standing uncorrected in the file — and the law does what the law said it would do: the agency files petitions to terminate your parental rights, citing fifteen of the last twenty-two months in care (42 U.S.C. § 675(5)(E)). The petitions are not the end of the case — termination must still be proven by clear and convincing evidence, grounds and needs-and-welfare both, at a hearing where everything in this scenario could still be built. But the case's center of gravity moves, permanently, from 'when do they come home' to 'whether you remain their father in law.'

Read the route that led here without flinching: the clock was known in January. What was missing was never love, time, or even cooperation — it was sequence. The March record unrequested; the narrower question unasked; the study unstarted while weeks did what weeks do. ASFA does not require families to be perfect. It requires the file to be built before the date, and it is pitiless about the difference between 'in progress' and 'documented.'

If you are living this ending: the petitions raise the stakes; they do not seal them. Build now what January asked for — the corrected record, the specified kinship plan, the children's own voices — and build it for a termination hearing's higher burden. Many fathers have. The calendar that hurt you is also the calendar that tells you exactly how much time the other side needs to prove its case. Use yours better.
